t: Jainism, taught by Mahavira in north-east India in the same age as the Buddha, holds that every living being has a soul and that release from rebirth comes through non-violence, truth and the renunciation of possessions.
Its monks and nuns live by five great vows of extreme strictness, while its lay followers, many of them merchants and bankers, became one of the most prosperous and influential communities of India.
Divided since about the 1st century CE into the Digambara and Svetambara traditions, it built temples of rare beauty and influenced Gandhi’s ideal of non-violence.
dyk: The colossal statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, carved from a single block of granite around 983, stands about 17 metres high and is anointed with milk, saffron and flowers every twelve years.
ev: Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, teaches in the Ganges valley, by Jain tradition
Mahavira attains omniscience and teaches the path of non-violence; he dies at Pavapuri
By Digambara tradition, Bhadrabahu leads monks to the south, joined by Chandragupta Maurya
King Kharavela of Kalinga honours the Jinas in his Hathigumpha inscription
The community divides into the Digambara and Svetambara traditions
A council at Valabhi writes down the Svetambara canon
The statue of Bahubali is carved at Shravanabelagola
King Kumarapala of Gujarat embraces Jainism under the teacher Hemachandra

f.origin: Magadha, north-east India, 6th or 5th century BCE
f.founder: Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, after Parshvanatha and twenty-two earlier teachers of the tradition
f.scriptures: The Agamas of the Svetambara canon; the Shatkhandagama and the works of Kundakunda for the Digambaras; the Tattvartha Sutra, accepted by both
f.followers: About 4.5 million in India (2011 census), with communities in Britain, North America and East Africa
